claim: Humans and animals can integrate sensory evidence from various sources to make decisions in a statistically near-optimal manner when stimulus presentation time is fixed across trials.
source: Humans and animals can integrate sensory evidence from various sources to make decisions in a statistically near-optimal manner, provided that the stimulus presentation time is fixed across trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Little is known about whether optimality is preserved when subjects can choose when to make a decision in reaction-time tasks.
source: Little is known about whether optimality is preserved when subjects can choose when to make a decision (reaction-time task), nor when sensory inputs have time-varying reliability.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Behavior is clearly sub-optimal when quantified with traditional optimality metrics that ignore reaction times in a reaction-time version of a visual/vestibular heading discrimination task.
source: Using a reaction-time version of a visual/vestibular heading discrimination task, we show that behavior is clearly sub-optimal when quantified with traditional optimality metrics that ignore reaction times.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: A computational model that accumulates evidence optimally across both cues and time, and trades off accuracy with decision speed, quantitatively explains subjects's choices and reaction times.
source: We created a computational model that accumulates evidence optimally across both cues and time, and trades off accuracy with decision speed. This model quantitatively explains subjects's choices and reaction times, supporting the hypothesis that subjects do, in fact, accumulate evidence optimally over time and across sensory modalities, even when the reaction time is under the subject's control.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Subjects accumulate evidence optimally over time and across sensory modalities, even when the reaction time is under the subject's control.
source: This model quantitatively explains subjects's choices and reaction times, supporting the hypothesis that subjects do, in fact, accumulate evidence optimally over time and across sensory modalities, even when the reaction time is under the subject's control.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model's ability to explain behavioral data.

claim: Subjects' ability to discriminate among stimuli improves when multiple sensory cues are available.
source: These studies generally reveal that subjects' ability to discriminate among stimuli improves when multiple sensory cues are available, such as visual and tactile (van Beers et al., 1996; Ernst and Banks, 2002), visual and auditory (Battaglia et al., 2003), or visual and vestibular (Fetsch et al., 2009) cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Performance gains associated with cue integration are generally well predicted by models that combine information across senses in a statistically optimal manner.
source: The performance gains associated with cue integration are generally well predicted by models that combine information across senses in a statistically optimal manner (Clark and Yuille, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cue integration is optimal if the information in the combined, multisensory condition is the sum of that available from the separate cues.
source: Specifically, we consider cue integration to be optimal if the information in the combined, multisensory condition is the sum of that available from the separate cues (see Supplementary file 1 for formal statement) (Clark and Yuille, 1990).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors based on prior work.

claim: Previous studies and models only consider situations in which the stimulus duration is fixed and subjects are required to withhold their response until the stimulus epoch expires.
source: Previous studies and models share a common fundamental limitation: they only consider situations in which the stimulus duration is fixed and subjects are required to withhold their response until the stimulus epoch expires.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior work in the field.

claim: Human performance is markedly suboptimal when evaluated with standard criteria that ignore reaction times in a reaction-time version of a multimodal heading discrimination task.
source: Indeed, using a reaction-time version of a multimodal heading discrimination task, we demonstrate here that human performance is markedly suboptimal when evaluated with standard criteria that ignore reaction times.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: The conventional framework for optimal cue integration is not applicable to behaviors in which decision times are under subjects' control.
source: Thus, the conventional framework for optimal cue integration is not applicable to behaviors in which decision times are under subjects' control.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Reaction times for multisensory stimuli are faster than predicted by 'parallel race' models in some studies.
source: Some of these studies have reported that reaction times for multisensory stimuli are faster than predicted by 'parallel race' models (Raab, 1962; Miller, 1982), suggesting that multisensory inputs are combined into a common representation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Other groups have failed to replicate findings that reaction times for multisensory stimuli are faster than predicted by parallel race models.
source: However, other groups have failed to replicate these findings (Corneil et al., 2002; Whitchurch and Takahashi, 2006) and it is unclear whether the sensory inputs are combined optimally.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Multisensory integration in reaction time experiments remains poorly understood.
source: Thus, multisensory integration in reaction time experiments remains poorly understood, and there is no coherent framework for evaluating optimal decision making that incorporates both perceptual sensitivity and reaction times.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: There is no coherent framework for evaluating optimal decision making that incorporates both perceptual sensitivity and reaction times.
source: Thus, multisensory integration in reaction time experiments remains poorly understood, and there is no coherent framework for evaluating optimal decision making that incorporates both perceptual sensitivity and reaction times.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Diffusion models have proven to be very effective at characterizing both the speed and accuracy of perceptual decisions for tasks based on information from a single sensory modality.
source: For tasks based on information from a single sensory modality, diffusion models (DMs) have proven to be very effective at characterizing both the speed and accuracy of perceptual decisions, as well as speed/accuracy trade-offs (Ratcliff, 1978; Ratcliff and Smith, 2004; Palmer et al., 2005) (where accuracy is used in the sense of percentage of correct responses).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The novel diffusion model integrates evidence optimally over time and across different sensory cues.
source: Here, we develop a novel form of DM that not only integrates evidence optimally over time but also across different sensory cues, providing an optimal decision model for multisensory integration in a reaction-time context.
evidence: This is a description of the model developed in the study.

claim: The model is capable of combining cues optimally even when the reliability of each sensory input varies as a function of time.
source: The model is capable of combining cues optimally even when the reliability of each sensory input varies as a function of time.
evidence: This is a description of the model's capabilities.

claim: The model reproduces human subjects' behavior very well.
source: We show that this model reproduces human subjects' behavior very well, thus demonstrating that subjects near-optimally combine momentary evidence across sensory modalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Subjects near-optimally combine momentary evidence across sensory modalities.
source: We show that this model reproduces human subjects' behavior very well, thus demonstrating that subjects near-optimally combine momentary evidence across sensory modalities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model's ability to reproduce behavior.

claim: The model predicts the counterintuitive finding that discrimination thresholds are often increased during cue combination.
source: The model also predicts the counterintuitive finding that discrimination thresholds are often increased during cue combination, and demonstrates that this departure from standard cue-integration theory is due to a speed-accuracy tradeoff.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the model.

claim: The departure from standard cue-integration theory (increased discrimination thresholds during cue combination) is due to a speed-accuracy tradeoff.
source: The model also predicts the counterintuitive finding that discrimination thresholds are often increased during cue combination, and demonstrates that this departure from standard cue-integration theory is due to a speed-accuracy tradeoff.
evidence: This is an explanation provided by the model.

claim: Seven human subjects (3 males) aged 23–38 years with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of vestibular deficits participated in the experiments.
source: Seven subjects (3 males) aged 23–38 years with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of vestibular deficits participated in the experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Heading discrimination performance improved with an increase in heading direction away from straight ahead for all conditions and all subjects.
source: For all conditions and all subjects, heading discrimination performance improved with an increase in heading direction away from straight ahead and with increased visual motion coherence.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data.

claim: Heading discrimination performance improved with increased visual motion coherence for all conditions and all subjects.
source: For all conditions and all subjects, heading discrimination performance improved with an increase in heading direction away from straight ahead and with increased visual motion coherence.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data.

claim: Discrimination thresholds consistently decreased with an increase in motion coherence for both the visual and combined conditions.
source: For both the visual and combined conditions, discrimination thresholds consistently decreased with an increase in motion coherence (Figure 2B for subject D2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for other subjects), indicating that increasing coherence improves heading discrimination.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Increasing coherence improves heading discrimination.
source: For both the visual and combined conditions, discrimination thresholds consistently decreased with an increase in motion coherence (Figure 2B for subject D2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for other subjects), indicating that increasing coherence improves heading discrimination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Traditional cue combination models predict that the discrimination threshold in the combined condition should be smaller than that of either unimodal condition.
source: Traditional cue combination models predict that the discrimination threshold in the combined condition should be smaller than that of either unimodal condition (Clark and Yuille, 1990).
evidence: This is a statement about predictions from prior models.

claim: With a fixed stimulus duration, the prediction that discrimination threshold in the combined condition should be smaller than that of either unimodal condition has been shown to hold for visual/vestibular heading discrimination in both human and animal subjects.
source: With a fixed stimulus duration, this prediction has been shown to hold for visual/vestibular heading discrimination in both human and animal subjects (Fetsch et al., 2009, 2011), consistent with optimal cue combination.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The discrimination thresholds of subjects in the reaction-time task appear to be substantially sub-optimal.
source: In contrast, the discrimination thresholds of subjects in our reaction-time task appear to be substantially sub-optimal.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data.

claim: For the example subject of Figure 2A, psychometric functions in the combined condition lie between the visual and vestibular functions.
source: For the example subject of Figure 2A, psychometric functions in the combined condition lie between the visual and vestibular functions.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Discrimination thresholds for the combined condition are intermediate between visual and vestibular thresholds for the example subject, and for high coherences, are substantially greater than the optimal predictions.
source: Correspondingly, discrimination thresholds for the combined condition are intermediate between visual and vestibular thresholds for this subject, and for high coherences, are substantially greater than the optimal predictions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In no case did subjects feature a significantly lower discrimination threshold in the combined condition than the better of the two unimodal conditions.
source: In no case did subjects feature a significantly lower discrimination threshold in the combined condition than the better of the two unimodal conditions (p>0.57, one-tailed, Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: For the largest visual motion coherence (70%), all subjects except one showed thresholds in the combined condition that were significantly greater than visual thresholds and significantly greater than optimal predictions of a conventional cue-integration scheme.
source: For the largest visual motion coherence (70%), all subjects except one showed thresholds in the combined condition that were significantly greater than visual thresholds and significant greater than optimal predictions of a conventional cue-integration scheme (p<0.05, Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The ratio of observed to predicted thresholds in the combined condition was significantly greater for subjects in the reaction-time task compared to human and monkey subjects performing a similar task in a fixed duration setting.
source: We found this ratio to be significantly greater for our subjects (Figure 2C; two-sample t test, t (77) = 3.245, p=0.0017).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of data from different studies.

claim: Subjects in the reaction-time task performed significantly worse than those engaged in a similar fixed-duration task with respect to predictions of standard multisensory integration models.
source: This indicates that, with respect to predictions of standard multisensory integration models, our subjects performed significantly worse than those engaged in a similar fixed-duration task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical comparison.

claim: Short reaction times imply that subjects gather less information to make a decision, yielding greater discrimination thresholds.
source: Short reaction times imply that subjects gather less information to make a decision, yielding greater discrimination thresholds.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between reaction time and discrimination threshold.

claim: Longer reaction times may decrease thresholds, but at the cost of time.
source: Longer reaction times may decrease thresholds, but at the cost of time.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the speed-accuracy tradeoff.

claim: If subjects decide more rapidly in the combined condition than the visual condition, they might feature higher discrimination thresholds in the combined condition even if they make optimal use of all available information.
source: Consequently, if subjects decide more rapidly in the combined condition than the visual condition, they might feature higher discrimination thresholds in the combined condition even if they make optimal use of all available information.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between reaction time and discrimination threshold.

claim: To assess if subjects perform optimal cue combination, we need to account for the timing of their decisions.
source: Thus, to assess if subjects perform optimal cue combination, we need to account for the timing of their decisions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the need for a new framework.

claim: Average reaction times depended on stimulus condition, motion coherence, and heading direction.
source: Average reaction times depended on stimulus condition, motion coherence, and heading direction.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data.

claim: Reaction times were faster for larger heading magnitudes.
source: In general, reaction times were faster for larger heading magnitudes, and reaction times in the vestibular condition were faster than those in the visual condition (Figure 3 for subject D2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for other subjects).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Reaction times in the vestibular condition were faster than those in the visual condition.
source: In general, reaction times were faster for larger heading magnitudes, and reaction times in the vestibular condition were faster than those in the visual condition (Figure 3 for subject D2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for other subjects).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: In the combined condition, reaction times were much shorter than those seen for the visual condition and were comparable to those of the vestibular condition.
source: In the combined condition, however, reaction times were much shorter than those seen for the visual condition and were comparable to those of the vestibular condition (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Subjects spent substantially more time integrating evidence in the visual condition, which boosted their discrimination performance when compared to the combined condition.
source: Thus, subjects spent substantially more time integrating evidence in the visual condition, which boosted their discrimination performance when compared to the combined condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reaction time and discrimination threshold data.

claim: Discrimination thresholds in the combined condition were substantially smaller than vestibular thresholds, especially at 70% coherence.
source: Note also that discrimination thresholds in the combined condition were substantially smaller than vestibular thresholds, especially at 70% coherence (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Adding optic flow to a vestibular stimulus decreased the discrimination threshold with essentially no loss of speed.
source: Thus, adding optic flow to a vestibular stimulus decreased the discrimination threshold with essentially no loss of speed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Subjects made use of both visual and vestibular information to perform the reaction-time task.
source: These data provide clear evidence that subjects made use of both visual and vestibular information to perform the reaction-time task, but the benefits of cue integration could not be appreciated by considering discrimination thresholds alone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The benefits of cue integration could not be appreciated by considering discrimination thresholds alone.
source: These data provide clear evidence that subjects made use of both visual and vestibular information to perform the reaction-time task, but the benefits of cue integration could not be appreciated by considering discrimination thresholds alone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The two unimodal DMs are combined optimally by weighting their rates of change in proportion to their relative sensitivities.
source: Rather, it can be shown that the two particle trajectories are combined optimally by weighting their rates of change in proportion to their relative sensitivities (see Supplementary file 1 for derivation):
evidence: This is a theoretical derivation presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model assumes that subjects know their cue sensitivities, kvis(c) and kvest, as well as the temporal sensitivity profiles, a(t) and v(t), of each stimulus.
source: The model assumes that subjects know their cue sensitivities, kvis(c) and kvest, as well as the temporal sensitivity profiles, a(t) and v(t), of each stimulus.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: The model provides an upper bound on performance, since subjects may not have perfect knowledge of cue sensitivities and temporal sensitivity profiles.
source: In this respect, our model provides an upper bound on performance, since subjects may not have perfect knowledge of these variables, especially since stimulus modalities and visual motion coherence values are randomized across trials ('Discussion').
evidence: This is a statement about the model's limitations.

claim: Varying the bound was essential to capture the deviation of the discrimination threshold in the combined condition from that predicted by traditional cue combination models.
source: Varying the bound was essential to capture the deviation of the discrimination threshold in the combined condition from that predicted by traditional cue combination models (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's ability to fit the data.

claim: The discrimination threshold is inversely proportional to bound and sensitivity.
source: Indeed, this discrimination threshold is inversely proportional to bound and sensitivity (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the model.

claim: Heading is represented by a neural population code in which neurons have heading tuning curves that differ in their heading preferences but have similar shapes within the range of heading tested.
source: We assumed that heading is represented by a neural population code in which neurons have heading tuning curves that, within the range of heading tested in this experiment (±16°, Figure 5A), differ in their heading preferences but have similar shapes.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model based on prior knowledge.

claim: The assumption of a neural population code for heading is broadly consistent with data from area MSTd.
source: This is broadly consistent with data from area MSTd (Fetsch et al., 2011), but the exact location of such a code is not important for our argument.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: For low coherence, motion energy in the stimulus is almost uniform for all heading directions, such that all neurons in the population fire at approximately the same rate.
source: For low coherence, motion energy in the stimulus is almost uniform for all heading directions, such that all neurons in the population fire at approximately the same rate (Figure 5A, dark blue curve).
evidence: This is an assumption of the model based on prior knowledge.

claim: For high coherence, population neural activity is strongly peaked around the actual heading direction.
source: For high coherence, population neural activity is strongly peaked around the actual heading direction (Figure 5A, cyan curve) (Morgan et al., 2008; Fetsch et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The variance of neural responses is proportional to their firing rate.
source: Since experimental data suggest that the variance of these responses is proportional to their firing rate (Tolhurst et al., 1983), the sum of the variances is proportional to the area underneath the population activity profile (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The scaling of the diffusion variance by coherence makes the prediction that reaction times for headings near straight ahead should be inversely proportional to coherence in the visual condition.
source: The above scaling of the diffusion variance by coherence, which is a consequence of the neural code for heading, makes an interesting prediction: reaction times for headings near straight ahead should be inversely proportional to coherence in the visual condition, even though the mean drift rate, kvis(c)sin(h), is very close to 0.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the model.

claim: Subjects tended to decide faster for higher coherences even when h ≈ 0.
source: This is indeed what we observed: subjects tended to decide faster for higher coherences even when h ≈ 0 (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in figures.

claim: This aspect of the data can only be captured by the model if the DM variance is allowed to change with coherence.
source: This aspect of the data can only be captured by the model if the DM variance is allowed to change with coherence (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's ability to fit the data.

claim: Observed reaction times were assumed to be composed of the decision time and some non-decision time.
source: Observed reaction times were assumed to be composed of the decision time and some non-decision time.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: The decision time is the time from the start of integrating evidence until a decision is made, as predicted by the diffusion model.
source: The decision time is the time from the start of integrating evidence until a decision is made, as predicted by the diffusion model.
evidence: This is a definition within the model.

claim: The non-decision time includes the motor latency and the time from stimulus onset to the start of integrating evidence.
source: The non-decision time includes the motor latency and the time from stimulus onset to the start of integrating evidence.
evidence: This is a definition within the model.

claim: Predicted and observed sensitivities for the combined condition are virtually identical.
source: Predicted and observed sensitivities for the combined condition are virtually identical (Figure 6), providing strong support for near-optimal cue combination across both time and cues.
evidence: This claim is based on model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: For low coherences at which optic flow provides no useful heading information, the sensitivity in the combined condition was not significantly different from that of the vestibular condition.
source: Remarkably, for low coherences at which optic flow provides no useful heading information, the sensitivity in the combined condition was not significantly different from that of the vestibular condition (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Subjects were able to completely suppress noisy visual information and rely solely on vestibular input, as predicted by the model.
source: Thus, subjects were able to completely suppress noisy visual information and rely solely on vestibular input, as predicted by the model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: For 8 of 10 datasets, the model explains more than 95% of the variance in the data (adjusted R² > 0.95).
source: For 8 of 10 datasets, the model explains more than 95% of the variance in the data (adjusted R2 > 0.95), providing additional evidence for near-optimal cue combination across both time and cues (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The model nicely captures the observation that the psychophysical threshold in the combined condition is typically greater than that for the visual condition, despite near-optimal combination of momentary evidence from the visual and vestibular modalities.
source: Critically, the model nicely captures the observation that the psychophysical threshold in the combined condition is typically greater than that for the visual condition, despite near-optimal combination of momentary evidence from the visual and vestibular modalities (e.g., Figure 3, 70% coherence, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Apparent sub-optimality in psychophysical thresholds can arise even if subjects combine all cues in a statistically optimal manner.
source: Thus, the model fits confirm quantitatively that apparent sub-optimality in psychophysical thresholds can arise even if subjects combine all cues in a statistically optimal manner, emphasizing the need for a computational framework that incorporates both decision accuracy and speed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: Subjects weight cues according to their relative sensitivities.
source: Together, these model variants strongly support the hypothesis that subjects weight cues according to their relative sensitivities, as given by Equation 2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: If we assumed that the temporal weighting of both modalities followed the acceleration profile of the stimulus while leaving the model otherwise unchanged, the model fit worsened decisively.
source: If we assumed that the temporal weighting of both modalities followed the acceleration profile of the stimulus while leaving the model otherwise unchanged, the model fit worsened decisively (Figure 7B, 'weighting by acceleration').
evidence: This claim is based on Bayesian model comparison.

claim: Assuming that the weighting of both modalities followed the velocity profile of the stimulus also decisively reduced fit quality.
source: Assuming that the weighting of both modalities followed the velocity profile of the stimulus also decisively reduced fit quality (Figure 7B, 'weighting by velocity'), although this effect was not consistent across subjects (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on Bayesian model comparison.

claim: If we completely removed temporal weighting of cues from the model, fits were dramatically worse than the optimal model.
source: If we completely removed temporal weighting of cues from the model, fits were dramatically worse than the optimal model (Figure 7B, 'no temporal weighting').
evidence: This claim is based on Bayesian model comparison.

claim: Subjects seem to be able to take into account their sensitivity to the evidence across time as well as across cues.
source: Thus, subjects seem to be able to take into account their sensitivity to the evidence across time as well as across cues.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: The parallel race model predicts that decisions in the combined condition are caused by the faster modality.
source: Because it does not combine information across modalities, the parallel race model predicts that decisions in the combined condition are caused by the faster modality.
evidence: This is a statement about the predictions of the parallel race model.

claim: Choices in the combined condition are unlikely to be more correct (on average) than those of the faster unimodal condition according to the parallel race model.
source: Consequently, choices in the combined condition are unlikely to be more correct (on average) than those of the faster unimodal condition.
evidence: This is a statement about the predictions of the parallel race model.

claim: For all but one subject, the vestibular modality is substantially faster, even when compared to the visual modality at high coherence and controlling for the effect of heading direction.
source: For all but one subject, the vestibular modality is substantially faster, even when compared to the visual modality at high coherence and controlling for the effect of heading direction (2-way ANOVA, p<0.0001 for all subjects except C).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: All subjects except subject C feature significantly lower psychophysical thresholds in the combined condition than in the vestibular condition.
source: Critically, all of these subjects feature significantly lower psychophysical thresholds in the combined condition than in the vestibular condition (p<0.039 for all subjects except subject C, p=0.210, Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Standard tests (Miller's bound and Grice's bound) revealed that all but two subjects made significantly slower decisions than predicted by the parallel race model for most coherence/heading combinations.
source: Furthermore, we performed standard tests (Miller's bound and Grice's bound) that compare the observed distribution of reaction times with that predicted by the parallel race model (Miller, 1982; Grice et al., 1984). These tests revealed that all but two subjects made significantly slower decisions than predicted by the parallel race model for most coherence/heading combinations (p<0.05 for all subjects except subjects F and B2; Supplementary file 2B), and no subject was faster than predicted (p>0.05, all subjects; Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The parallel race model can be rejected as a viable hypothesis to explain the observed behavior.
source: Based on these observations, we can reject the parallel race model as a viable hypothesis to explain the observed behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical tests.

claim: When subjects are allowed to choose how long to accumulate evidence in a cue integration task, their behavior no longer follows the standard predictions of optimal cue integration theory that normally apply when stimulus presentation time is controlled by the experimenter.
source: We have shown that, when subjects are allowed to choose how long to accumulate evidence in a cue integration task, their behavior no longer follows the standard predictions of optimal cue integration theory that normally apply when stimulus presentation time is controlled by the experimenter.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Subjects feature worse discrimination performance (higher psychophysical thresholds) in the combined condition than would be predicted from the unimodal conditions—in some cases even worse than the better of the two unimodal conditions.
source: Particularly, they feature worse discrimination performance (higher psychophysical thresholds) in the combined condition than would be predicted from the unimodal conditions—in some cases even worse than the better of the two unimodal conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Subjects tend to decide more quickly in the combined condition than in the more sensitive unimodal condition and thus have less time to accumulate evidence.
source: This occurs because subjects tend to decide more quickly in the combined condition than in the more sensitive unimodal condition and thus have less time to accumulate evidence.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed behavior.

claim: A more general definition of optimal cue integration must incorporate reaction times.
source: This indicates that a more general definition of optimal cue integration must incorporate reaction times.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings.

claim: Subjects' behavior could be reproduced by an extended diffusion model that takes into account both speed and accuracy.
source: Indeed, subjects' behavior could be reproduced by an extended diffusion model that takes into account both speed and accuracy, thus suggesting that subjects accumulate evidence across both time and cues in a statistically near-optimal manner (i.e., with minimal information loss) despite their reduced discrimination performance in the combined condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Subjects accumulate evidence across both time and cues in a statistically near-optimal manner (i.e., with minimal information loss) despite their reduced discrimination performance in the combined condition.
source: Indeed, subjects' behavior could be reproduced by an extended diffusion model that takes into account both speed and accuracy, thus suggesting that subjects accumulate evidence across both time and cues in a statistically near-optimal manner (i.e., with minimal information loss) despite their reduced discrimination performance in the combined condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: Previous work on optimal cue integration was based on experiments that employed fixed-duration stimuli and was thus able to ignore how subjects accumulate evidence over time.
source: Previous work on optimal cue integration (e.g., Ernst and Banks, 2002; Battaglia et al., 2003; Knill and Saunders, 2003; Fetsch et al., 2009) was based on experiments that employed fixed-duration stimuli and was thus able to ignore how subjects accumulate evidence over time.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior work in the field.

claim: Previous work relied on the implicit assumption that subjects make use of all evidence throughout the duration of the stimulus.
source: Moreover, previous work relied on the implicit assumption that subjects make use of all evidence throughout the duration of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior work in the field.

claim: The assumption that subjects make use of all evidence throughout the duration of the stimulus need not be true and has been shown to be violated even for short presentation durations.
source: However, this assumption need not be true and has been shown to be violated even for short presentation durations (Mazurek et al., 2003; Kiani et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Apparent sub-optimality in some previous studies of cue integration or in some individual subjects might be attributable to either truly sub-optimal cue combination, to subjects halting evidence accumulation before the end of the stimulus presentation period, or to the difficulty in estimating stimulus processing time.
source: Therefore, apparent sub-optimality in some previous studies of cue integration or in some individual subjects (Battaglia et al., 2003; Fetsch et al., 2009) might be attributable to either truly sub-optimal cue combination, to subjects halting evidence accumulation before the end of the stimulus presentation period, or to the difficulty in estimating stimulus processing time (Stanford et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation about the causes of sub-optimality in prior studies.

claim: These potential causes cannot be distinguished using a fixed-duration task.
source: Unfortunately, these potential causes cannot be distinguished using a fixed-duration task.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of fixed-duration tasks.

claim: Allowing subjects to register their decisions at any time during the trial alleviates the confound of not knowing when subjects stop accumulating evidence.
source: Allowing subjects to register their decisions at any time during the trial alleviates this potential confound.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of reaction-time tasks.

claim: Based on behavioral data, parallel race models can be ruled out, as they cannot explain lower psychophysical thresholds (better sensitivity) in the combined condition relative to the faster vestibular condition.
source: Based on our behavioral data, we can rule out parallel race models, as they cannot explain lower psychophysical thresholds (better sensitivity) in the combined condition relative to the faster vestibular condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Neurophysiological studies demonstrate that visual and vestibular cues to heading converge in various cortical areas, including areas MSTd, VIP, and VPS.
source: Further evidence against such models is provided by neurophysiological studies which demonstrate that visual and vestibular cues to heading converge in various cortical areas, including areas MSTd (Gu et al., 2006), VIP (Schlack et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2011b), and VPS (Chen et al., 2011a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Activity in area MSTd can account for sensitivity-based cue weighting in a fixed-duration task.
source: Activity in area MSTd can account for sensitivity-based cue weighting in a fixed-duration task (Fetsch et al., 2011), and MSTd activity is causally related to multi-modal heading judgments (Britten and van Wezel, 1998, 2002; Gu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Physiological studies strongly suggest that visual and vestibular signals are integrated in sensory representations prior to decision-making, inconsistent with parallel race models.
source: These physiological studies strongly suggest that visual and vestibular signals are integrated in sensory representations prior to decision-making, inconsistent with parallel race models.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior physiological studies.

claim: The model makes the assumption that sensory signals are integrated prior to decision-making and is in this sense similar to co-activation models.
source: Our model makes the assumption that sensory signals are integrated prior to decision-making and is in this sense similar to co-activation models that have been used previously to model reaction times in multimodal settings (Miller, 1982; Corneil et al., 2002; Townsend and Wenger, 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's assumptions and relationship to prior models.

claim: Co-activation models have been introduced to explain reaction times that are faster than those predicted by parallel race models.
source: First, co-activation models have been introduced to explain reaction times that are faster than those predicted by parallel race models (Raab, 1962; Miller, 1982).
evidence: This is a statement about prior models.

claim: Subjects in the current study feature reaction times that are slower than those of parallel race models in almost all conditions.
source: Our subjects, in contrast, feature reaction times that are slower than those of parallel race models in almost all conditions (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data.

claim: The model captures the effect of slower reaction times than parallel race models by an elevated effective bound in the combined condition as compared to the faster vestibular condition, such that cue combination remains optimal despite longer reaction times.
source: We capture this effect by an elevated effective bound in the combined condition as compared to the faster vestibular condition, such that cue combination remains optimal despite longer reaction times.
evidence: This is a statement about how the model explains the data.

claim: Co-activation models usually combine inputs from the different modalities by a simple sum.
source: Second, co-activation models usually combine inputs from the different modalities by a simple sum (e.g., Townsend and Wenger, 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about prior models.

claim: Combining inputs from different modalities by a simple sum entails adding noise to the combined signal if the sensitivity to one of the modalities is low, which is detrimental to discrimination performance.
source: This entails adding noise to the combined signal if the sensitivity to one of the modalities is low, which is detrimental to discrimination performance.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of simple summation.

claim: Different cues need to be weighted according to their sensitivities to achieve statistically optimally integration of multisensory evidence at each moment in time.
source: In contrast, we show that different cues need to be weighted according to their sensitivities to achieve statistically optimally integration of multisensory evidence at each moment in time (Equation 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's approach.

claim: Serial race models can be ruled out by observing that they predict reaction times in the combined condition to be longer than those in the slower of the two unimodal conditions.
source: Another alternative to co-activation models are serial race models, which posit that the race corresponding to one cue needs to be completed before the other one starts (e.g., Townsend and Wenger, 2004). These models can be ruled out by observing that they predict reaction times in the combined condition to be longer than those in the slower of the two unimodal conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the predictions of serial race models.

claim: Serial race models are clearly violated by the subjects' behavior.
source: This is clearly violated by the subjects' behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Optimal accumulation of evidence over time requires the momentary evidence to be weighted according to its associated sensitivity.
source: Optimal accumulation of evidence over time requires the momentary evidence to be weighted according to its associated sensitivity.
evidence: This is a theoretical result presented in the manuscript.

claim: For the vestibular modality, the temporal profile of sensitivity to the evidence follows acceleration.
source: For the vestibular modality, we assume that the temporal profile of sensitivity to the evidence follows acceleration.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: Neural activity in response to self-motion in multimodal areas MSTd, VIP, and VPS reflects a mixture of velocity and acceleration components.
source: This may appear to conflict with data from multimodal areas MSTd, VIP, and VPS, where neural activity in response to self-motion reflects a mixture of velocity and acceleration components (Fetsch et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2011a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The vestibular stimulus is initially encoded by otolith afferents in terms of acceleration.
source: Note, however, that the vestibular stimulus is initially encoded by otolith afferents in terms of acceleration (Fernandez and Goldberg, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Any neural representation of vestibular stimuli in terms of velocity requires a temporal integration of the acceleration signal, and this integration introduces temporal correlations into the signal.
source: Thus, any neural representation of vestibular stimuli in terms of velocity requires a temporal integration of the acceleration signal, and this integration introduces temporal correlations into the signal.
evidence: This is a logical inference about neural processing.

claim: A neural response that is maximal at the time of peak stimulus velocity does not imply a simultaneous peak in the information coded about heading direction.
source: As a consequence, a neural response that is maximal at the time of peak stimulus velocity does not imply a simultaneous peak in the information coded about heading direction.
evidence: This is a logical inference about neural coding.

claim: Information still follows the time course of its original encoding, which is in terms of acceleration.
source: Rather, information still follows the time course of its original encoding, which is in terms of acceleration.
evidence: This is a logical inference about neural coding.

claim: The time course of the sensitivity to the visual stimulus is less clear.
source: In contrast, the time course of the sensitivity to the visual stimulus is less clear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge.

claim: The model assumes the sensitivity to the visual stimulus follows the velocity profile of the stimulus, as information per unit time about heading certainly increases with the velocity of the optic flow field, even when there is no acceleration.
source: For our model we have intuitively assumed it to follow the velocity profile of the stimulus, as information per unit time about heading certainly increases with the velocity of the optic flow field, even when there is no acceleration.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model based on intuition.

claim: The assumption that visual sensitivity follows the velocity profile is supported by a decisively worse model fit if we set the weighting of the visual momentary evidence to follow the acceleration profile.
source: This assumption is supported by a decisively worse model fit if we set the weighting of the visual momentary evidence to follow the acceleration profile (Figure 7B, 'weighted by acceleration').
evidence: This claim is based on model comparison.

claim: The model fits make clear that temporal weighting of vestibular and visual inputs is necessary to predict behavior when stimuli are time-varying.
source: In any case, our model fits make clear that temporal weighting of vestibular and visual inputs is necessary to predict behavior when stimuli are time-varying.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: The extended DM model makes the strong assumption that cue sensitivities are known before combining information from the two modalities, as these sensitivities need to be known in order to weight the cues appropriately.
source: The extended DM model described here makes the strong assumption that cue sensitivities are known before combining information from the two modalities, as these sensitivities need to be known in order to weight the cues appropriately.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's assumptions.

claim: It is possible that subjects can estimate their sensitivity (as influenced by coherence) during the initial low-velocity stimulus period in which heading information is minimal but motion coherence is salient.
source: As only the sensitivity to the visual stimulus changes across trials in our experiment, it is possible that subjects can estimate their sensitivity (as influenced by coherence) during the initial low-velocity stimulus period (Figure 1C) in which heading information is minimal but motion coherence is salient.
evidence: This is speculation about how subjects might estimate sensitivity.

claim: For the task in this study, it is reasonable to assume that subjects can estimate their sensitivity to cues.
source: Thus, for our task, it is reasonable to assume that subjects can estimate their sensitivity to cues.
evidence: This is a statement about the reasonableness of the model's assumptions.

claim: Conventional definitions of optimality do not apply to cue integration tasks in which subjects' decision times are unconstrained.
source: In closing, our findings establish that conventional definitions of optimality do not apply to cue integration tasks in which subjects' decision times are unconstrained.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Human behavior is broadly consistent with predictions of how sensory evidence should be weighted across modalities and time to achieve optimal performance in reaction-time tasks, but not with alternative models.
source: We establish how sensory evidence should be weighted across modalities and time to achieve optimal performance in reaction-time tasks, and we show that human behavior is broadly consistent with these predictions but not with alternative models.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The findings and the extended diffusion model provide the foundation for building a general understanding of perceptual decision-making under more natural conditions in which multiple cues vary dynamically over time and subjects make rapid decisions when they have acquired sufficient evidence.
source: These findings, and the extended diffusion model that we have developed, provide the foundation for building a general understanding of perceptual decision-making under more natural conditions in which multiple cues vary dynamically over time and subjects make rapid decisions when they have acquired sufficient evidence.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the work.
